title: Switched-Capacitor Amplifiers
intro: With the switch errors understood, three SC amplifiers can be compared: the unity-gain sampler, the non-inverting amplifier and the precision multiply-by-two. For each, the clock timing removes signal-dependent charge injection, and the feedback factor sets the gain error and the settling time (Razavi, Section 13.3).

blocks.text: Capacitors on a chip

A metal-insulator-metal or stacked-metal capacitor has a parasitic capacitance $C_p$ from its bottom plate to the substrate, typically 5 to 10% of its value, and a much smaller one from the top plate. Circuits are therefore drawn so that the bottom plate is always driven (by the input or the op-amp output) and the top plate faces the sensitive op-amp input.
Unity-gain sampler

blocks.alt: Schematic. Vin passes switch S1 to node P, then capacitor CH to node X at the op amp's minus input (plus input grounded). Switch S2 connects X to the output; switch S3 connects P to the output.
blocks.caption: Sample with S1 and S2; hold by flipping $C_H$ around the op amp with S3.

blocks.text: Sampling: S1 and S2 on, X is a virtual ground and $C_H$ tracks $V_{in}$. Hold: S2 turns off first, then S1, then S3 closes and $C_H$ sits in the feedback loop, so $V_{out} \approx V_0$, the input at the instant S2 opened.

Why the timing matters: when S2 opens, X is at virtual ground, so its channel charge is the same for every input; it causes only an offset, which a differential version removes (with an extra equalising switch between the two X nodes to cancel the mismatch of the two reset switches). After S2 is open, X floats and its total charge is frozen. Any charge S1 then injects at P cannot change the final output, because once the loop settles X is again a virtual ground and charge conservation at X forces $V_{out} = 0$ for that disturbance. The charge S3 needs to turn on comes from the op amp, not from $C_H$.

Speed

In the sampling phase the time constant is $\tau_{sam} = (R_{on1} + 1/G_m)C_H$, since the op amp in unity feedback presents about $1/G_m$ at X. In the hold phase the op amp, modelled as $G_m$ with output resistance $R_0$, driving $C_L$, settles with

blocks.caption: Independent of $R_0$: more output resistance means more loop gain, which leaves the closed-loop speed unchanged.

blocks.text: At the start of the hold phase X jumps to about $-V_0$, so the op amp may slew first: its tail current steers fully to one side and the output ramps at about $I_{SS}/C_L$ until X comes back near its final value, then linear settling with $\tau_{amp}$ takes over. $C_{in}$ hurts both speed and precision, which is another reason the capacitor's top plate goes to X (bottom-plate sampling), also keeping substrate noise off X. Compared with a plain switch and capacitor followed by a buffer, the flip-around sampler is slower but its charge injection is input-independent.
Non-inverting amplifier

The two-phase amplifier of the fundamentals page ($C_1$ sampled, then its left plate grounded so its charge moves to $C_2$) gives a gain of $C_1/C_2$ with the same polarity as the input. Again S2 (the reset) opens first and sets the sampling instant; afterwards P is a driven node that goes from one fixed voltage ($V_{in0}$) to another (ground), so injection by S1, the charge S3 absorbs, and any input movement after S2 opens all wash out. Its accuracy and speed:

Read the time constant as an op amp of transconductance $G_m$ reduced by the feedback factor $\beta = C_2/(C_1 + C_2 + C_{in})$, driving $C_L$ in parallel with $C_2$ in series with $C_1 + C_{in}$. Both the gain error and $\tau$ grow with the nominal gain $C_1/C_2$. For unity gain ($C_1 = C_2 = C_H$) the error is twice that of the unity-gain sampler, whose feedback factor is $C_H/(C_H + C_{in})$ instead of about 1/2. With $C_L = 0$, $\tau = (C_1 + C_{in})/G_m$, independent of $C_2$.
Precision multiply-by-two

blocks.alt: Schematic. Vin drives two switches S1 and S2 to the left plates of equal capacitors C1 and C2, whose right plates join at node X, the op amp's minus input. S3 connects X to the output. S4 connects the left plate of C1 to the output; S5 grounds the left plate of C2.
blocks.caption: Both capacitors sample; then $C_1$ becomes the feedback capacitor and $C_2$ gives up its charge to it.

blocks.text: Both equal capacitors sample $V_{in}$ (total charge $2CV_{in0}$). In amplification S3 opens first, $C_1$ is flipped around the op amp and $C_2$'s left plate is grounded, so $C_2$ empties into $C_1$ and $V_{out} \approx 2V_{in0}$. The gain error and time constant follow the non-inverting formulas, but the feedback factor is about 1/2 instead of 1/3 for a gain of two, so it is faster and more accurate. The cost is twice the input capacitance during sampling. As with the others, only S3's charge matters, and it is a constant.

blocks.title: Required op-amp gain
blocks.text: A unity-gain sampler has $C_H = 1.5$ pF and $C_{in} = 0.3$ pF. What op-amp gain keeps the gain error below 0.05%?

blocks.title: Settling time constants
blocks.text: With $G_m = 5$ mS and $C_L = 1$ pF, find $\tau_{amp}$ for (a) the unity-gain sampler with $C_H = 1.5$ pF, $C_{in} = 0.3$ pF; (b) a non-inverting gain-of-four stage with $C_1 = 2$ pF, $C_2 = 0.5$ pF, $C_{in} = 0.2$ pF.
solution: (b) $C_1 + C_{in} = 2.2$ pF: numerator $= 1 \times 2.2 + 1 \times 0.5 + 2.2 \times 0.5 = 3.8$ pF²; $\tau = 3.8\text{ pF}^2/(5\text{ mS} \times 0.5\text{ pF}) = 1.52$ ns.
